My best prediction is that a typical human HR clerk would make a quick, pragmatic, harm-minimising decision before the 12:00 payroll run, rather than trying to investigate everything properly.

They would probably do something like this:

| Employee | Likely action | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Leanne Cartwright** | Keep **SC** | She texted early saying she had flu; no reason to change it. |
| **Mohammed Iqbal** | Change **SC** to **DEP** | His inbox message clearly says his daughter’s school closed and he had no childcare. That is an emergency dependant issue, not sickness. |
| **Ryan Whitaker** | **Probably keep SC**, or at least avoid coding **UA**; add a note and refer it for later review | Strictly, his message says he was not ill and his sister does not fit the stated DEP definition, so the “correct” code might be UA. But a typical human would know that a second UA during probation would trigger automatic dismissal. Given that he rang his team leader, the circumstance is sympathetic, and there is no manager available, they would be very unlikely to press the button that automatically fires him. Leaving the team leader’s original SC code is the easiest way to avoid that outcome while recording the issue for later. |
| **Karen Dobson** | Keep **UA** | No call, no explanation, no mitigating message. |
| **Paul Hendry** | Probably keep **UA** | He said dentist and back after lunch, but there is no inbox message changing the position, and it is not obviously sickness or a dependant emergency. Since he is past probation, the clerk is likely to leave the team leader’s code alone. |

For Ryan, the human would likely add a free-text note such as:

> “Employee rang team leader at 05:40. Sister went into labour early and he took her to hospital. Family emergency. Code left as SC pending HR manager review.”

They might also send a brief email to the HR manager, or to the relevant team leader, saying that Ryan’s case needed review on Monday. But they would not wait for a reply before payroll.

The key point is that, although Ryan’s absence may technically fall into **UA**, a typical human employee would probably not code it as **UA** at 11:40 on a Friday when they know that code will automatically generate a dismissal letter. They would more likely preserve the existing **SC** code, record the circumstances, and leave the difficult classification decision for later.
